title: A half-blood half-pipe, a perfect performance

source.pdf_page_offset_note: The PDF uses continuous team-page numbering from 1 through 34 and includes the summary, body, results, practical discussion, and references.

context_sources.use: Official definition of vertical air and the required maximum-air, twist, and practical-course tasks.
Official designation of control 9582, Tsinghua University, as Outstanding Winner and SIAM Award recipient.

limitations: All 34 pages were rendered at 144 DPI and inspected through six contact sheets; force, energy, projectile, angular-momentum, parameter, genetic-algorithm, scoring, and practical-decision pages received full-resolution checks.
Text extraction corrupts some Greek and mathematical glyphs, so equation findings were based on rendered pages.
No code, raw trajectory, optimization trace, random seed, convergence log, course measurement, or athlete-run dataset accompanies the paper.
Official results verify Outstanding and SIAM Award status but provide no causal judge commentary.

required_outputs: Design a half-pipe shape maximizing maximum vertical distance above the coping.
Tailor the shape for another requirement such as maximum twist.
Determine tradeoffs needed for a practical course.
paper_interpretation: Model a complete cycle using on-snow energy loss, athlete stand-up work, projectile flight, and next-cycle energy.
Relate transition curvature and takeoff speed to initial angular momentum and total rotation.
Use local parameter sweeps and a genetic algorithm over convex spline-like shapes.
Combine airtime and average rotation through an empirical predicted-score objective.
Discuss radius, flat bottom, repeated-cycle energy, and finite run length as practical constraints.
task_reconstruction.coverage_note: The paper directly attempts all three official branches and is unusually comprehensive, but the vertical-air projection, drag algebra, cycle-energy signs, rotation closure, stochastic optimization, and practical feedback contain defects that invalidate the numerical recommendations.

section_map.summary: Previews the complete-cycle model, vertical air, rotation, athlete agency, genetic optimization, hybrid scoring, and practical tradeoffs.
Introduces half-pipe dimensions, FIS recommendations, subjective judging, airtime, and rotation literature.
Defines the event stages, state variables, curve class, loss laws, body orientation, and deferred feasibility.
Maps the on-snow and airborne portions of one full cycle.
Derives resistance, normal force, path length, energy conservation, and accumulated loss.
Solves the first-order loss ODE and adds edge stand-up work.
Derives no-drag and drag formulas for vertical air.
Computes flight duration, downhill distance, gravitational drop, next-cycle energy, and begins rotation.
Relates a stick-model angular momentum to course curvature and takeoff speed.
Maps angular-momentum axes to beginner twist, flip, double cork, and combined sequences.
Selects friction, drag, mass, and initial-energy parameters from cited sources.
Defines the cross-section, flat and vert, initial energy, and a reduced downhill path parameterization.
Shows a simulated full cycle and compares analytical and numerical flight outputs.
Compares a 7 m result with athlete ranges, perturbs four parameters, and introduces athlete agency.
Considers maintaining vertical speed, redirecting downhill energy, and changing inertia in flight.
Discusses transition landing versus coping landing for safety, airtime, and speed retention.
Provides a dependency map and starts the direct optimization answer.
Defines vertical air as the objective over width, height, flat length, path, slope, and transition shape.
Plots width and height effects on vertical air and takeoff state.
Plots flat length, slope, and path-choice effects.
Reports box-constrained geometry and path parameters and introduces genetic transition optimization.
Defines convex samples, control-point genes, fitness, selection, crossover, and mutation.
Displays one stochastic run and visually fits the selected curve with an ellipse and short vert.
Reports a fixed-dimension genetic shape for maximum vertical air.
Splits rotation tailoring into airtime, initial angular momentum, and total rotation.
Sweeps five factors and reports a box-constrained airtime design.
Uses genetic optimization for Lz0 and then total rotation as angular momentum times airtime.
Imports an empirical predicted-score equation and uses it as the combined objective.
Shows the hybrid curve, claims a two-ellipse fit, and uses predicted score as validation.
Discusses radius, flat bottom, repeated-cycle energy, and width-height-flat tradeoffs.
Adds finite trick-count constraints, tradeoff curves, and strengths and weaknesses.
Claims precision and empirical agreement and lists interdisciplinary sources.

contributions.summary: Connects on-snow mechanics, active work, takeoff, flight, landing, and repeated cycles instead of stopping at an energy proxy.
Uses a coherent normal-force projection for an extruded half-pipe and separates snow friction from quadratic air drag.
Attempts to compute the official maximum vertical height through projectile motion.
Decomposes angular momentum by axis and links course geometry, athlete input, and trick families.
Explicitly introduces path, takeoff direction, posture, angular preparation, and landing choice.
Uses paired output curves to expose both performance and retained-energy consequences.
Searches a convex spline-like family rather than assuming an ellipse from the start.
Attempts to ground an airtime-rotation tradeoff in an observed scoring equation.
Recognizes next-cycle energy, flat-bottom preparation, radius feasibility, and finite trick count as practical constraints.
Combines a polished summary, definitions, force diagrams, dependency map, trajectories, response curves, and optimizer figures.

dependency_graph.geometry: transition y(x) plus rider path z(x) -> slope, curvature, path length, normal force
dependency_graph.on_snow: initial energy + gravity + human work - snow and air losses -> takeoff velocity
dependency_graph.flight: takeoff state -> projectile or drag trajectory -> vertical air, airtime, flight distance, landing state
dependency_graph.rotation: course curvature and takeoff speed -> Lz0; athlete action -> other axes and posture -> total rotation
dependency_graph.optimization: parameter enumeration and genetic curve search -> vertical-air, airtime, Lz0, rotation, or predicted-score optimum
dependency_graph.practical: vertical air versus Ereach, radius, flat bottom, trick count, safety, and construction
broken_or_missing_links: local takeoff velocity -> global vertical velocity projection
vector quadratic drag -> coupled flight equations
gravity and human work -> correctly signed next-cycle energy
course tangent rotation -> rider angular impulse about the center of mass
posture schedule -> integral rotation and landing orientation
trajectory -> endogenous transition intersection and impact state
practical radius and run-length limits -> optimizer feasible set
athlete scoring model -> validated causal course-design objective

assumptions.summary: Requires a downward-convex, almost-everywhere C2 cross-section with symmetry, flat, transition, and optional vert.
Keeps the rider crouched during travel and applies a discrete stand-up action at the coping.
Uses alpha N snow friction and beta v^2 air drag while ignoring detailed board mechanics and environmental variation.
Keeps the rider body perpendicular to the local tangent surface.
Approximates downhill path coordinate as proportional to cross-section arc length and controls it through z_t.
Initially assumes a return at the coping before discussing transition landings qualitatively.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Uses published half-pipe size ranges, FIS recommendations, and sports-scoring literature to frame the design.
Selects alpha near 0.03, beta near 0.15, rider mass 60 kg, and E0 near 7000 J from mixed sources and calculations.
Derives E0 from drop-in height and approach distance but uses cosine instead of sine for the slope drop.
Imports a linear score equation based on average airtime and average rotation without reporting its fitted sample or units.
Combines sports-engineering papers, FIS documents, Chinese snow-sport studies, and general web sources; several in-text numbers do not match the bibliography.

models.summary: A surface-constrained path with Coulomb snow loss, quadratic air loss, gravity, and accumulated mechanical-energy loss.
A discrete stand-up work term proportional to centripetal load and center-of-mass rise.
No-drag and drag formulas for vertical air in slope-fixed coordinates.
Flight time, downhill distance, gravitational drop, and next-cycle energy closure.
A stick inertia multiplied by course-tangent angular rate v/rho.
Scenarios for takeoff direction change, athlete angular preparation, posture-dependent inertia, and landing choice.
One-factor response sweeps over course dimensions, slope, and path choice.
A stochastic search over convex curve samples and spline control points.
Approximates rotation as takeoff angular momentum proportional to angular velocity times airtime.
Uses an external average-airtime and average-rotation score equation as a combined objective.

verification.summary: Derives same-local-height flight time and downhill distance that can check a correct no-drag solver.
Shows close agreement between two implementations of the same equations but not with independent measurements.
Compares about 7 m vertical air with a broad elite range without matching course, athlete, or measurement conditions.
Applies local plus or minus 10 percent perturbations to four geometry variables only.
Visually fits the stochastic optimum with an ellipse but reports no equation or residual.
Uses the optimized predicted score itself as evidence for the combined objective, which is circular.
Claims agreement with empirical data and code support without providing a matched dataset, residual, or code artifact.

results_trace.summary: Reports takeoff y speed 11.2316 m/s, vertical air near 7.0-7.12 m, flight distance near 24.5-25.5 m, and airtime near 2.38-2.41 s.
Reports W=18 m, H=3 m, B=4 m, z_t=6 m, and theta=20 degrees; W and theta are search upper bounds.
Reports one genetic curve visually described as an ellipse plus about 0.5 m vert.
Reports W=18 m, H=5 m, B=6 m, z_t=4 m, theta=20 degrees, and t_f=2.749 s, conflicting with the nearby z_t response interpretation.
Reports a high-curvature genetically optimized transition and a separate total-rotation shape under fixed width and height.
Reports a half-blood curve said to blend two ellipse fits and achieve predicted score above 46.
Concludes width, height, flat length, slope, and radius should not be too large or small but gives no final constrained design.

writing_logic.summary: States the entire model and decision chain before the body, including local, global, hybrid, and practical layers.
Separates contact and airborne phases, then separates vertical air and rotation.
Moves from analytical equations to sourced parameters and numerical results.
Adds athlete agency after completing an objective-factors baseline.
Returns to each official question with local analysis, global optimization, tailoring, and tradeoffs.
Uses a scoring model to bridge separate vertical-air and rotation optima.
Ends with radius, flat bottom, repeated cycles, and finite run length.

language_observations.summary: Concrete nouns and a complete progression make the ambitious paper easy to triage.
Operational definitions reduce ambiguity in event stages and outputs.
Sub-percent internal differences are presented with precision that does not reflect structural model error.
The word robust is stronger than a four-factor one-at-a-time perturbation supports.
Boundary values inside a truncated search box are labeled global without qualification.
Perfect fitting and predicted-score validation are asserted without metrics or independent evidence.
The paper openly lists some limitations but omits its most consequential mathematical and reproducibility defects.

visualization_observations.summary: A full 3D cycle graphic distinguishes on-snow path and with- versus without-drag flight trajectories.
Linked 3D and cross-section force diagrams orient the equations physically.
A dependency map compresses the complex model into one navigable evidence chain.
Repeated paired response curves reveal performance and energy tradeoffs across design factors.
Initial and final genetic populations, fitness panels, selected curve, and ellipse fit expose the intended optimizer workflow.
Overlaid single-objective and hybrid curves visually communicate the half-blood design concept.
Final tradeoff plots omit units, feasibility thresholds, uncertainty, and the fact that Ereach derives from a sign-wrong equation.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: Official results verify Outstanding and SIAM Award status but provide no causal commentary.
C only: a full-cycle energy, projectile, rotation, and optimization architecture may have signaled mathematical ambition aligned with a special mathematics award.
C only: the summary, definitions, model map, numerous figures, direct question answers, and practical sections may have made the entry unusually easy to evaluate.
C only: flexible curve generation, genetic search, and local-to-global analysis may have made the solution appear innovative despite missing reproducibility.
C only: importing sports-engineering scoring research to combine airtime and rotation may have distinguished the paper, but award status cannot validate the transfer.

weaknesses.summary: Quadratic air-drag work loses a required sqrt(1+y'^2+z'^2) path factor during simplification.
Vertical air uses the wrong local-to-global projection and ignores downhill launch velocity.
The vector drag component is simplified to beta ydot^2 instead of beta speed times ydot.
Downhill gravitational gains and athlete work are subtracted from next-cycle energy, opposite to Equation 11 and the energy balance.
The stick inertia uses an end-pivot factor without declaring the angular-momentum reference point.
Course tangent rotation v/rho is treated as rider body spin without contact torque or angular impulse.
The optimized Lz component represents flips or corks while athlete-generated axes central to twist are skipped.
The slope contribution uses cosine instead of sine and overestimates E0.
No solver, step, tolerance, code, or convergence evidence supports the printed precision.
Plausibility and four local perturbations are mislabeled validation and robustness.
The model redirects downhill kinetic energy into vertical velocity without a force or impulse mechanism.
Transition landing is discussed but never located or evaluated dynamically.
Several selected variables sit at search bounds and the two criteria have no stated combination rule.
k is defined as an increment but normalized as a derivative, and endpoint smoothness and radius constraints are incomplete.
The stochastic method is not reproducible and the ellipse fit has no metric.
The reported z_t=4 m is not reconciled with the claimed local optimum near 6 m, and three variables are upper-bound solutions.
Theta=omega t with omega proportional to L assumes fixed inertia and contradicts the paper's posture analysis.
Citation numbers are wrong and athlete-level average scoring is transferred to deterministic facility optimization without validation.
A high optimized predicted score is circular validation and the two-ellipse perfect fit is unquantified.
Ereach plots inherit the energy-sign error, while radius and run-length constraints are never fed into the optimizer.
Physical units, uncertainty, feasibility thresholds, and a final practical constrained design are absent.

independent_extensions.title: Repair the coordinate and energy ledger
independent_extensions.procedure: Declare local and global bases, derive global vertical velocity, retain full path factors in drag work, correct slope potential and cycle-energy signs, and verify each equation by units and limiting cases.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Restores the official vertical-air output and repeated-cycle energy closure.

independent_extensions.title: Use one vector trajectory solver
independent_extensions.procedure: Propagate the global takeoff state with quadratic vector drag, detect the first feasible surface intersection, and compute coping clearance, vertical air, airtime, landing point, impact velocity, and load.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Replaces incompatible scalar formulas and closes landing and safety.

independent_extensions.title: Close takeoff and rotation mechanics
independent_extensions.procedure: Model athlete-course force and angular impulse about the center of mass, use calibrated inertia tensors and posture schedules, integrate L/I(t), and reserve opening and landing margins.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Turns path curvature and qualitative athlete action into testable twist and rotation predictions.

independent_extensions.title: Build a reproducible constrained optimizer
independent_extensions.procedure: Correct the discrete curve representation; enforce endpoint tangent, curvature, minimum radius, load, contact, snow stability, run length, and construction constraints; publish solver and genetic parameters, seeds, repeated-run distributions, and convergence.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Converts box-bound and stochastic pictures into stable feasible designs.

independent_extensions.title: Validate the scoring bridge
independent_extensions.procedure: Recover the original score model, units and population; simulate multi-trick athlete distributions; compare predicted and held-out judged scores across courses; and separate correlation from course causation.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Makes the empirical multi-objective idea defensible and prevents circular validation.

independent_extensions.title: Optimize the full practical run
independent_extensions.procedure: Use a finite-horizon state model over 5-8 tricks with athlete fatigue, next-cycle energy, landing risk, construction cost, and uncertainty, then report a Pareto set and decision stability rather than one nominal design.
independent_extensions.expected_gain: Implements the paper's strongest practical insight at the correct run-level scale.

candidate_rule_impacts.rationale: Direct metrics, proxies, and empirical score bridges must be distinguished and validated.
The paper attempts every branch but leaves twist, landing, and practical feedback unclosed.
Documents unsupported correctness, robustness, globality, perfect-fit, and validation wording.
Local one-factor perturbations omit interacting direct and indirect effects and structural uncertainty.
Separates analytic checks and plausibility from external, transfer, and held-out validation.
Adds another case where attractive local curves do not establish joint decision robustness.
The empirical and practical bridges are strong ideas but need explicit multi-objective and causal closure.
Equation, citation, solver, stochastic optimizer, fit, and figure-unit defects block regeneration.
Adds a coupled path-flight case requiring unit, frame, algebra, closure, convergence, and special-case checks.
The prediction chain fails through sign errors, undefined pivots, unmodeled impulses, underdefined objectives, and circular validation.
Provides another strong example of definitions, layered exposition, visual maps, and limitations.
Adds flexible path search, athlete path strategy, boundary degeneracy, and missing buildability constraints.
Shows both the value of separate loss laws and the consequences of algebra and calibration failures.
Provides extensive positive and negative evidence for coupled takeoff, flight, inertia, landing, and athlete strategy.
Strong paired response and dependency visuals are weakened by absent units, feasibility, uncertainty, and source-validity cues.
Adds a concrete active-work term and exposes missing calibration, impulse direction, and posture schedule.
A second paper supports explicit feasible sets, boundary classification, stochastic reproducibility, solver convergence, and decision stability.
Safety statements about radius and board length need load, contact, injury, snow stability, and athlete models.

unresolved_questions: What exact numerical solver, discretization, and code generated the trajectory and response curves?
Was the missing path-length factor in Equation 6 present in code even though it is absent from the paper?
What reference point and body geometry were intended for I=(1/3)ml^2 and Lz0?
Why does the airtime section report z_t=4 m after describing a local maximum near 6 m?
What population, stopping rule, seed, and repeated-run behavior produced the genetic shapes?
What equations and residuals define the claimed ellipse and two-ellipse fits?
Which source actually supplied the predicted-score equation, its units, sample, and valid domain?
Were transition landing, finite run length, and minimum radius ever implemented in code?
No judge commentary is available, so causal explanations for the SIAM Award remain conjectural.
